PicoSAS compared with widely used programs

Updated 2026-10-08. We give the same data files to PicoSAS and to BioXTAS RAW [3], FreeSAS [4], McSAS3 [5] and DENSS [6], and compare every result with a trusted reference: the values the SASBDB [1, 2] authors got with ATSAS [10], the mass from the protein sequence, or the known make-up of the sample. The protein datasets come from SASBDB entries we never used while developing PicoSAS. We chose them before testing, and ran each test once.

Reading the q unit from the file

Data files store q in 1/Å or in 1/nm, and many don't say which. Reading it wrong makes every size come out ten times too big or too small. Here we check that PicoSAS works out the unit from the file by itself; the other programs need you to set it.

PicoSAS read the q unit correctly on 108 of 108 test datasets, without being told.

Radius of gyration (Guinier)

The radius of gyration (Rg) is the overall size of a particle, read from the low-q part of the curve, the Guinier region [7]. It's usually the first number people check, and later steps such as P(r) and 3D start from it. The hard part is choosing the right range of points automatically, as AutoRG does in ATSAS [10] and RAW [3].

108 protein datasets from SASBDB [1, 2] that we never used while developing PicoSAS, compared with the Guinier Rg published by their authors.

Maximum dimension (P(r))

Dmax is the largest distance inside the particle, read from the pair-distance distribution P(r) [8]. It tells you how long or stretched-out the particle is. Choosing Dmax is partly a matter of judgement, so the programs differ more here than for Rg.

Molecular weight (Porod volume)

The molecular weight from a single curve, without knowing the concentration. It tells you whether a protein is on its own, in pairs or clumped together. The Porod volume method [9, 10] estimates the particle's volume and turns it into a mass.

Volume fraction from an absolute curve

The volume fraction is how much of the sample is taken up by particles. On an absolute intensity scale, the total scattering (the Porod invariant [9]) gives it directly. It matters for composites and powders, where the amount of filler is the question.

PicoSAS and McSAS3 [5] got the same datasets and the same contrast (BAM MOUSE series of YSZ in PEGDA [12, 13]).

3D shape from a curve

A low-resolution 3D shape built from the curve alone. We check two things: how well the model fits the measured data (χ²), and how close its shape is to the real atomic structure (NSD [11]; 0 is identical, around 1 or less is a good match).

Eleven SASBDB entries [1, 2] with a published ATSAS model [10], compared with PicoSAS and DENSS [6]. We compare the shape on the eight that also have an atomic structure.

Examples you can reproduce

Numbers alone don't show what a shape looks like, so here are three proteins of different sizes. Each row shows the same object four ways, seen from the front and from above: the atomic structure, the model the SASBDB authors built with ATSAS [10], the model PicoSAS built from the same curve, and the PicoSAS model as a see-through shell with the protein chain drawn inside. All four are turned to the same orientation, the way NSD [11] compares them. The settings under each figure are all you need to get the same model yourself.

Grey: the atomic structure deposited with the SASBDB entry. Blue: the authors' model. Orange: PicoSAS. The dark line is the protein chain, one point per amino acid. Each model is drawn at its true size; the bar shows the scale. PicoSAS runs the reconstruction 3 times and shows the most typical run. How close the runs are to each other (their NSD) tells you how far to trust the shape: stable below 0.6, fair up to 1, and unreliable above that.

Made with PicoSAS build 2026-10-05-v0.1. Running the same build with the same settings twice gave exactly the same model. On another computer the last digits may differ slightly.
